# Pricing Experiments in B2B

Source: https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-02 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Price is the strongest profit lever most firms have and the one they test least. A 1992 Harvard Business Review analysis of 2,463 companies found a 1% price improvement lifted operating profit by 11.1%, more than any other lever. B2B firms rarely have the volume or the anonymity for consumer-style A/B tests, so this piece sets out the experiments that do work: cohort changes, packaging tests, discount guardrails and stated-preference research, with the record each one needs and the competition-law line not to cross.

A pricing experiment is a deliberate, recorded change to price, packaging or discount rules, made for a defined group of customers or deals, with a measure and a date to judge it. B2B firms seldom have the volume or the anonymity to run consumer-style A/B tests on list price, but they can test price for new cohorts, test packaging, test discount guardrails and run structured buyer research. The payoff is large: Marn and Rosiello's 1992 analysis of 2,463 companies found a 1% price improvement lifted operating profit by 11.1%. The discipline is the same as any test: decide in advance what result would change the decision.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Most mid-size B2B firms change their prices rarely and test them almost never. A price list is set during a planning cycle, discounts fill the gap between the list and what buyers will pay, and nobody can say afterwards whether the list was right.

The reluctance is understandable. B2B buyers talk to each other, contracts run for years, and a single large deal can swamp a quarter's results. But the alternative to testing is not stability. It is a price set by the accumulated discounts of individual sellers, which is a test nobody designed and nobody reads.

## Why price deserves the effort

The case rests on arithmetic that has held for three decades.

Michael Marn and Robert Rosiello's 1992 *Harvard Business Review* article, "Managing Price, Gaining Profit", used the average economics of 2,463 companies in the Compustat database. A 1% improvement in price raised operating profit by 11.1%. The same improvement in variable cost raised it by 7.8%, in volume by 3.3% and in fixed cost by 2.3%.

McKinsey's 2026 analysis of 10-K filings from 140 listed distribution companies reached a similar conclusion in one sector: a 1% price increase was associated with a more than 22% boost in EBITDA margin.

| Lever, 1% improvement | Effect on operating profit (Marn and Rosiello, 1992) |
| --- | --- |
| Price | 11.1% |
| Variable cost | 7.8% |
| Volume | 3.3% |
| Fixed cost | 2.3% |

These are averages across very different firms, and the exact multiplier depends on margin. The ranking is what matters. For most firms, a small, durable improvement in realised price is worth more than a large effort on volume.

## Where the money actually leaks

Marn and Rosiello's second contribution was the pocket price waterfall: the sequence of discounts, rebates, payment terms and allowances between list price and what the firm actually keeps. They found the same product selling across a wide band of pocket prices, 35% from highest to lowest in one of their examples.

McKinsey's 2026 distribution research describes the same pattern in modern form. One building materials distributor's sales teams had been overriding system prices in more than half of transactions. After changes to pricing tools and rules, it cut manual overrides by 80% and expanded margins by more than 200 basis points.

Most mid-size firms can draw their own waterfall from data they already hold: list price from the price book, invoice price from billing, and the deductions in between from contracts and credit notes. The first version is usually rough, but even a rough waterfall shows which deductions are largest and which are granted most inconsistently.

That points to where a mid-size firm should start. The first experiments are rarely about list price. They are about the discount rules, approval thresholds and packaging decisions that determine how far realised price falls below it. Part 21 of this series covered discount governance; this piece is about testing whether those rules are right.

> The alternative to testing price is not stability. It is a price set by every seller's last discount.

## Experiments that work at B2B volumes

Consumer firms can show two prices to two random groups and count conversions. Most B2B firms cannot: volumes are too low, buyers compare notes, and showing two customers different prices for the same thing creates a fairness problem that outlasts the test. The methods below are designed around those constraints.

| Method | What it tests | Fits when | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New-cohort price change | A new list price or rate for new customers only, from a set date | Steady flow of new deals; existing contracts protected | Comparison with earlier cohorts is confounded by market changes |
| Packaging test | A new tier, bundle or add-on, offered alongside the current one | Several offers already exist; buyers choose | Cannibalising the current offer |
| Discount guardrail test | A tighter discount limit or approval threshold for one segment, team or region | Discounting is frequent and recorded | Sellers route deals around the rule |
| Staggered renewal increase | A price change applied at renewal in waves | Renewal base is large enough to stagger | Churn in the first wave is read too early |
| Stated-preference research | Willingness to pay from structured interviews or surveys, such as Van Westendorp or Gabor-Granger questions, or conjoint analysis | Before a launch or major change | What buyers say differs from what they pay |

Four rules make any of these readable.

**Decide the decision first.** Write down what result would lead you to keep, extend or reverse the change, before the test starts. In [*Tests that close questions*](https://lowob.com/research/tests-that-close-questions/) we argued that a test without a pre-stated decision rule rarely ends; it gets reinterpreted.

**Pick a comparison.** A hold-out segment, an earlier cohort, or a matched set of deals from the same quarter. A B2B test seldom needs statistical perfection, but it does need a reasonable answer to "compared with what?". The answer matters more than it looks: Gordon, Zettelmeyer and colleagues compared common observational measurement methods with 15 randomised advertising experiments at Facebook and found the observational methods generally overestimated the effect, though sometimes they underestimated it. A before-and-after reading of a price change carries the same risk.

**Do not read the result early.** Fix the check date and hold to it. Johari, Pekelis and Walsh showed that repeatedly checking a test and stopping at the first favourable reading can raise the false positive rate fivefold, even at 10,000 observations. Price tests run on far fewer, so an early reading is even less reliable.

**Measure realised price, not only win rate.** A test that raises win rate while lowering average realised price may have found a discount, not a better price. Track win rate, average discount, realised price and, where the cycle allows, early retention.

## Reading the evidence you already have

Many firms already hold the data for a first experiment. They have simply not read it as one.

Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmarks, built from 4.2 million opportunities, found that offering a discount early in the cycle was associated with a 39% drop in win rates. That is a vendor correlation, not a controlled result: deals that need early discounts may be weaker deals. It is a hypothesis, and a cheap one to test. Hold the discount back until a defined stage in one segment for a quarter, and compare win rate and realised price with a segment that kept the old rule.

Everstage's 2026 survey of 195 North American revenue leaders found 47% took three or more days to approve a pricing exception. Approval delay is itself a pricing variable. A faster route for exceptions within a band, and a slower one outside it, can be tested like any other rule.

Pricing models are also moving. Metronome's 2026 review of more than 50 AI and software pricing models found hybrid pricing, mixing subscriptions with usage, credits or overages, to be the norm, and noted one company that made four major pricing structure changes in under two years. For firms considering usage or outcome pricing, [*Seats, usage or outcomes*](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) sets out the trade-offs; packaging tests are how to try them without betting the base.

## The legal and fairness line

Testing your own prices is ordinary commercial practice. Two lines need care.

**Competitors' data.** In November 2025 the US Department of Justice announced a proposed settlement with RealPage, a pricing-software provider, over allegations that pooling competitors' non-public, competitively sensitive data to generate pricing recommendations violated Section 1 of the Sherman Act. Paul, Weiss's analysis of the settlement draws practical lessons: risk is highest where current or forward-looking non-public competitor data feeds recommendations, auto-accept features should be opt-in, and the user should keep the decision. A firm's own data and its own tests are treated differently. The rule for a pricing experiment is simple: its inputs are your own prices, costs and outcomes, and public information.

**Price discrimination.** Charging different customers different prices is lawful in most B2B contexts, but not all. In the US, the Robinson-Patman Act restricts some forms of price discrimination between competing purchasers of goods, which matters for firms selling through resellers or distributors. The FTC's guidance sets out the tests: the Act applies to commodities, not services, to goods of like grade and quality sold to at least two purchasers around the same time, and only where competition may be injured. Its two main defences are a price difference justified by cost and a concession made in good faith to meet a competitor's price. Take advice before testing different prices on customers who compete with each other.

Fairness is a commercial constraint as well as a legal one. Buyers compare notes, and a customer who learns they paid more for the same thing during a test is a renewal risk. Tests on new cohorts, packaging and internal rules avoid most of that exposure.

## The record every experiment needs

A pricing experiment is a commercial decision with an unusually clear outcome, and it belongs in the record with the same fields as any other: the change, the reason, the owner, the group affected, the expected result and decision rule, the check date, and the outcome written back.

The record matters more for pricing than for most decisions because pricing knowledge decays fast. Two years after a test, the people who ran it may have gone, and the next team will rerun it. A recorded test, superseded rather than overwritten when the price changes again, is how a firm builds its own evidence on what buyers will pay.

Illustrative example: testing a discount guardrail

Decision
:   For one quarter, require approval for any discount offered before the proposal stage in the mid-market segment; leave the enterprise segment on the existing rule.

Reason and owner
:   Recorded deals showed early discounts were common in mid-market and win rates were no higher where they were given. Owned by the revenue lead, with finance agreeing the decision rule in advance: keep the change if win rate falls by less than three points and average realised price rises.

What changed
:   Win rate, average discount and realised price are compared across the two segments at quarter end, and the result is written to the record.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Price is the strongest lever.** A 1% improvement in realised price beats a 1% gain in volume by a wide margin.
- **Start with leakage.** Discount rules, overrides and packaging usually matter more than list price.
- **Design for B2B constraints.** New cohorts, packaging, guardrails and staggered renewals avoid the fairness problem of random price tests.
- **Stay on your own data.** Never feed competitors' non-public prices into a pricing decision.

Gateway card

### Before you run a pricing experiment

- The change, the group affected and the comparison group written down
- A decision rule agreed with finance before the test starts
- Realised price and discount tracked, not only win rate
- Existing contracts and competing resellers checked for legal or fairness exposure
- Inputs limited to your own data and public information
- A check date and an outcome field in the record

## Common questions

### Can you A/B test prices in B2B?

Rarely in the consumer sense, because volumes are low and buyers compare notes. B2B firms usually test with new-customer cohorts, packaging options, discount rules or staggered renewal changes instead.

### How much does a 1% price increase affect profit?

In Marn and Rosiello's 1992 analysis of 2,463 companies, a 1% price improvement raised operating profit by 11.1% on average, against 3.3% for a 1% gain in volume. The effect depends on a firm's margin.

### What is a pocket price waterfall?

The sequence of discounts, rebates, payment terms and allowances between list price and the revenue a firm actually keeps from a transaction. Marn and Rosiello introduced it to show where realised price leaks.

### Is it legal to charge B2B customers different prices?

Generally yes, but some rules apply, such as the US Robinson-Patman Act for competing purchasers of goods, and competition law forbids using competitors' non-public pricing data. Take legal advice for your market.
